title: Abuse of Information Repositories for Data Collection
shortTitle: Abuse of Information Repositories for Data Collection
summary: This strategy covers the abuse of information repositories for collection, tracked as T1213, where an adversary with a valid account harvests documents, tickets, wiki pages and code from collaboration platforms instead of from file servers. It matters because these platforms concentrate design documents, credentials in notes and incident detail in one searchable place, and because the traffic is ordinary authenticated application use that endpoint tools cannot see. The telemetry that makes detection possible is application level: representational state transfer interface audit logs from the collaboration platform, single sign on or identity provider logs with the session and device that started the access, message and file download events from the chat platform, and repository audit records for bulk clone or export operations. The main way it fails is that the platform logs are high volume and the abusive pattern is a legitimate user reading legitimate pages, so detection depends on per account behavioural baselines rather than signatures, and on correlating a single session across several platforms.

beginner.definition: Information repositories are shared tools where teams keep documents, notes, tickets and code. Examples are a wiki, a ticketing system, a chat tool and a code host. This detection looks for an account searching and downloading far more from those tools than it normally does. It catches collection, which happens before data leaves the company.
beginner.whyItMatters: These tools hold the story of how your company works. Plans, keys written in notes and incident details all live there. Access uses a normal login, so no endpoint alarm sounds. Staff often have broad read rights by design. Spotting a bulk harvest early lets you close the account before the data is shared outside.
howItWorks: Each collaboration platform keeps an audit record of who viewed, searched, exported or downloaded a page or item.
Those records are sent to the central log platform together with the login record from the identity provider.
The rule builds a normal pattern for each account: how many items a day, from which tools, at which hours.
It then looks for outliers. An example is hundreds of page views in one hour.
It links events from different platforms that share the same login session or the same device identifier.
When one session touches several repositories in a heavy way, the alert shows the account, the session and the items.
beginner.example: Think of a library reading room. Members may read any book on the shelf, and the librarian keeps a note of what leaves the room. One member asks for the same shelf, then the archive, then the basement store, all in one afternoon. No single request is against the rules. The shape of the afternoon tells the librarian that something unusual is going on.
takeaways: Repository logs are the only reliable place to see this collection, because the traffic is normal web use.
You need a per account baseline of item count and tool mix to separate work from harvest.
One login session that spans several platforms is a strong sign of a scripted collection.

objectives: Identify which collaboration platforms in your estate expose usable audit records.
Explain the difference between a large legitimate review and a scripted bulk harvest.
Join platform audit records with identity provider session data on session or device fields.
Build per account baselines for item views, exports and downloads.
Recognise export and repository clone operations that indicate whole workspace collection.
Describe the steps to take when a harvest is confirmed, including account review and notification.
dataSources: Collaboration platform audit log entries for page views, searches, exports and workspace downloads with actor account and client address
Identity provider sign in log with session identifier, device detail and multi factor authentication result for the same actor
Code hosting audit records for repository clone, archive download and personal access token use
Chat platform message export and file download events with channel, actor and file name
Ticketing or document management access log recording bulk search queries and result set sizes
logic: The pattern is one authenticated identity generating an unusually high number of item views, search queries or export operations across one or more repositories within a single session, especially when the items span projects the account has never touched and the client address or device has not been seen for that account before. The fields to correlate are the actor account, the session identifier and device identifier from the identity provider, the object or project identifiers from each platform audit log, and the volume of events per session. A normal user reads deeply in a handful of projects they belong to and returns to the same pages, while collection is wide, shallow and spread across unrelated projects with export or download calls at the end. The distinguishing factor is breadth across projects that the account has no stated role in.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk document harvest across collaboration repositories
# logsource:
#   product: gcp
#   service: workspace
# detection:
#   selection_view:
#     EventType: ['view', 'search', 'download_export']
#   selection_export:
#     EventType: 'export_workspace'
#   filter_service:
#     ActorEmail|endswith: '@vendor.example'
#   condition: selection_view or selection_export and not filter_service | count() by ActorEmail, SessionId > 300 in 1h
# level: high
falsePositives: Legal hold or electronic discovery processing where a small team exports a large document set under supervision
An employee preparing a handover or leaving the company who revisits every project they worked on in one week
Migration projects where an integration account reads all pages of a workspace to copy them into a new platform
Auditors reviewing a full year of tickets and documents during an annual assessment window
Onboarding sessions where a new joiner reads a very large amount of documentation in their first days
tuningNotes: Start with the export and workspace download events, which are few and high value, and treat them as the first rule because the signal to noise ratio is already good. Then add the volume rule for views and searches, filtered to accounts in sensitive groups and joined to sessions that lack a managed device or come from an unapproved network. Filter the documented migration, audit and discovery service accounts by name, and require a human owner to re approve those filters each quarter because they are the most likely place for an attacker to hide. Baseline item counts per account per hour for a month before enabling alerting, and set the threshold above the ninety ninth percentile of that account's own history rather than a global number. The coverage you give up with per account thresholds is a genuinely slow harvest that stays just under the account's own baseline, which is why a monthly report on widening project breadth is worth keeping alongside the alert.
